title: Chichinga with Suya Spice Blend
author: Eric Adjepong
desc: A chef's two-blend system — the suya is toasted first until it darkens slightly and smells nutty and toasty, three to five minutes.
longDesc: This is the most elaborate documented chichinga, built on two separate spice blends the chef keeps on hand. The suya blend alone runs to ten bouillon cubes, anise seeds, cloves, five grains of selim, a cup of peanut butter powder, a quarter cup of cayenne and three tablespoons each of ginger, garlic, paprika and onion powder — and crucially it is toasted in a dry pot before use until it darkens slightly and smells nutty and toasty. Two pounds of sirloin pounded to a quarter inch, cut into inch squares, three to a skewer with red and yellow peppers and red onion.
ingredients: 3/4 cup suya spice blend, plus more for garnish
// All-day seasoning blend, makes a scant 3/4 cup
equipment: Dry pot, for toasting the suya
steps: Combine the all-day seasoning blend ingredients.
Combine the suya spice blend ingredients.
Toast the suya in a pot over medium-low heat until it has darkened slightly and smells nutty and toasty, 3 to 5 minutes.
Pound the steak to a quarter inch thick and cut into 1-inch squares.
Coat the meat with the ginger garlic puree, all-day seasoning, salt, tomato paste, paprika and half the suya.
Skewer about 3 pieces of sirloin per skewer with the onion and peppers.
Mix the remaining suya with the oil and brush over the skewers.
Refrigerate 1 hour, then bring to room temperature.
Grill hot, turning and basting, until the vegetables and meat are slightly charred and the vegetables are tender, 5 to 8 minutes total.
Garnish with more suya and sea salt.
chefTips: Toast the suya blend first. Until it darkens slightly and smells nutty and toasty, three to five minutes — this is the step that separates a chef's suya from a shop-bought one, and it transforms the raw peanut powder.
Pound the sirloin to a quarter inch before cutting. Thin squares cook through in the five to eight minutes the vegetables need.
Half the suya into the meat, half mixed with oil as a baste. Two applications, and the second one is what crusts.
Refrigerate an hour, then bring back to room temperature before grilling. Cold meat on a hot grill chars outside and stays raw inside.
The doneness cue covers both components: slightly charred meat AND tender vegetables. The vegetables are the slower of the two.
Ten bouillon cubes in the blend is a lot of salt, so go carefully with the extra tablespoon and a half.
Both blends keep, which is the point of making them — the all-day seasoning makes a scant three quarters of a cup and is useful far beyond this dish.
commonMistakes: Meat thicker than a quarter inch.
All the suya into the marinade, leaving nothing to baste with.
Over-salting on top of ten bouillon cubes.
sources: Adapted from 'Chichinga' by Eric Adjepong, from Ghana to the World (Clarkson Potter, 2025; photographs by Doaa Elkady), via The Local Palate, 12 May 2025, 'Reprinted with permission'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches and were identical (TWO-PASS). Yield as printed: serves 6-8. Equipment as printed: 8 to 10 metal or wooden skewers.

All-Day Seasoning Blend exactly as printed, making a scant ¾ cup: 1 tablespoon dried parsley; 1 tablespoon dried oregano; 1 tablespoon salt; 2 teaspoons dried thyme; 2 teaspoons dried rosemary; 2 teaspoons whole black peppercorns; 1 teaspoon cumin seeds; ¼ teaspoon cayenne pepper; ¼ cup sweet paprika; 3 tablespoons granulated garlic; 2 tablespoons granulated onion; 2 teaspoons Worcestershire powder (optional).

Suya Spice Blend exactly as printed: 10 Maggi seasoning cubes; 1½ teaspoons anise seeds; ½ teaspoon whole cloves; 5 grains of Selim; 1 cup unsweetened peanut butter powder; ¼ cup cayenne pepper; 3 tablespoons ground ginger; 3 tablespoons garlic powder; 3 tablespoons sweet paprika; 3 tablespoons onion powder. The brand name is rendered generically as bouillon cubes above.

Chichinga exactly as printed: 2 pounds sirloin steak; 3 tablespoons ginger garlic puree; 2 tablespoons All-Day Seasoning Blend; 1½ tablespoons salt; 2 teaspoons tomato paste; 1 teaspoon sweet paprika; ¾ cup Suya Spice Blend, plus more for garnish; 1/3 cup neutral oil; 2 medium red onions, ½-inch dice; 2 red bell peppers; 2 yellow bell peppers; Sea salt for garnish.

THE TOASTING CUE, verbatim and the best technique note across the three documented chichinga: toast the suya over medium-low 'until the suya has darkened slightly and smells nutty and toasty, 3 to 5 minutes'.
THE GRILLING CUE, verbatim: grill 'until the vegetables and meat are slightly charred and the vegetables are tender, 5 to 8 minutes total'.

A MISSING UNIT, flagged and NOT corrected: the grill temperature prints as 'about 550' WITH NO UNIT. In context it is almost certainly degrees Fahrenheit, but the source does not say so and no figure is asserted above.
HEADNOTE, verbatim: 'These are the quintessential Ghanaian kebabs, but really they belong to most West African homes.'

THIS IS A NEW NAMED GHANAIAN AUTHOR in the documented record — Eric Adjepong, whose 2025 cookbook is one of very few in-print Ghanaian cookbooks whose recipes are retrievable at all. Newspaper and magazine serialisation is what made it reachable, the same route that made Zoe Adjonyoh's and Lopè Ariyo's recipes available.
For the three-way disagreement between the documented chichinga — beef with tankora, sirloin with a toasted two-blend suya, and goat with a wet ground-peanut rub — see the sources at GHA061.
storage: Best at once. The blends keep for months in sealed jars.
reheating: Briefly on a hot grill or under a broiler.
healthBenefits: Sirloin is high in protein, iron, zinc and vitamin B12.
Peanut butter powder gives the peanut flavour with far less fat than paste.
Red and yellow peppers are very high in vitamin C.
Grilled rather than fried, with the oil used only as a baste.
culturalNote: Keeping two standing spice blends and toasting one before use is a restaurant approach to a street food, and it is how a chef makes a charcoal-grill flavour reproducible in a home kitchen. The bouillon cubes in the suya are not a shortcut but how the blend is actually made across West Africa.
